```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# Global chunk options control how code and output appear in the HTML file.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  comment = NA,
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5
)
```

# Aim

This document demonstrates the main RMarkdown features you will need in this module:

- section headings,
- R code chunks,
- inline R code,
- loading packages and data,
- rendering tables and figures,
- cross-referencing tables and figures,
- citing a source from a `.bib` file,
- rendering the document to HTML.

RMarkdown is useful because it keeps text, code, results, and figures in one reproducible document. This idea is closely related to literate programming [@knuth1984literate] and dynamic documents [@xie2017dynamic].

# Load Packages

```{r packages}
# tidyverse gives us read_csv(), select(), drop_na(), summarise(), arrange(), and ggplot().
library(tidyverse)

# knitr gives us kable(), which creates simple tables in rendered documents.
library(knitr)
```

# Load Data

We will use the `blomkvist.csv` dataset. The data are stored in the local `data` folder for this week.

```{r load-data}
# Read the CSV file and store it in an object called blomkvist.
blomkvist <- read_csv("data/blomkvist.csv")
```

The dataset contains `r nrow(blomkvist)` rows and `r ncol(blomkvist)` columns. Inline R code is useful when values should update automatically if the data change.

# Inspect Data

Table \@ref(tab:data-preview) shows rows 1 to 6 of the dataset.

```{r data-preview, echo=FALSE}
# slice() can select rows by position. Here we keep rows 1 to 6.
first_rows <- slice(blomkvist, 1:6)

# kable() turns a data frame into a formatted table in the HTML output.
kable(
  first_rows,
  caption = "Rows 1 to 6 of the Blomkvist dataset."
)
```

# Prepare Data

Here we keep a few variables and remove missing reaction-time values.

```{r prepare-data}
# Keep only the variables used in this short report.
selected_data <- select(
  blomkvist,
  id,
  sex,
  age,
  smoker,
  rt_hand_d,
  rt_hand_nd
)

# Remove rows with missing values in either reaction-time variable.
plot_data <- drop_na(selected_data, rt_hand_d, rt_hand_nd)
```

After removing missing values, the plotting dataset contains `r nrow(plot_data)` rows.

# Create a Figure

Figure \@ref(fig:scatter-plot) shows the relationship between reaction times for the dominant and non-dominant hand. The plot is included directly from the R code chunk.

```{r scatter-plot, fig.cap="Reaction times for dominant and non-dominant hand responses."}
# Start with the data and define the variables used in the plot.
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = rt_hand_d, y = rt_hand_nd, colour = smoker)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Dominant hand reaction time",
    y = "Non-dominant hand reaction time",
    colour = "Smoking status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Create a Summary Table

Table \@ref(tab:summary-table) summarises the dominant-hand reaction times by smoking status.

```{r summary-table}
# Calculate descriptive statistics for each smoking-status group.
summary_table <- summarise(
  plot_data,
  mean_rt = round(mean(rt_hand_d), 1),
  sd_rt = round(sd(rt_hand_d), 1),
  n = n(),
  .by = smoker
)

# Put the table rows into a predictable order.
summary_table <- arrange(summary_table, smoker)

# Render the summary data frame as a table in the HTML output.
kable(
  summary_table,
  caption = "Dominant-hand reaction time by smoking status."
)
```

# Interpretation

The average dominant-hand reaction time in the cleaned dataset is `r round(mean(plot_data$rt_hand_d), 1)` ms. When writing up visualisations, combine code-generated values with a short explanation of what the plot or table shows.

# How to Render

To render this document in RStudio:

1. Click **Knit**.
2. Check that the output HTML file appears in the same folder.
3. Open the HTML file and check that the table, figure, citations, and references appear correctly.
